title: Limits & Continuity
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The limit is the foundation of calculus — the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point, even if undefined there. Formal definition: lim(x→a) f(x) = L. One-sided limits (from left/right). A function is continuous at a point if the limit equals the function's value (no jumps, holes, or asymptotes). Techniques: direct substitution, factoring to cancel, rationalizing, and L'Hôpital's rule for indeterminate forms (0/0, ∞/∞). Limits at infinity describe end behavior. The limit formalizes 'approaching' rigorously, making instantaneous rates definable.

WORKED EXAMPLE: lim(x→2) (x²−4)/(x−2). Direct substitution gives 0/0 (indeterminate). Factor: (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x+2. Now substitute: 2+2 = 4. The hole at x=2 is 'removable' — the limit exists (4) even though the function is undefined there. This is the essence of limits: what the function approaches, not what it equals.

PRACTICE: 1) Evaluate lim(x→3)(x²−9)/(x−3). 2) Determine if f(x)=1/x is continuous at x=0. 3) Find lim(x→∞) (3x²+1)/(x²+5).

title: Derivatives & Differentiation Rules
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The derivative f'(x) is the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the tangent line, defined as the limit of the difference quotient. Rules: power rule (d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹), constant, sum, product rule (fg)' = f'g + fg', quotient rule, and the chain rule for composite functions (the most important: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x)). Derivatives of trig, exponential (eˣ is its own derivative), and logarithmic functions. Higher-order derivatives (acceleration is the second derivative of position). Implicit differentiation for curves not solved for y.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Differentiate f(x) = (3x² + 1)⁵ using the chain rule. Outer: 5(...)⁴; inner derivative: 6x. So f'(x) = 5(3x²+1)⁴ · 6x = 30x(3x²+1)⁴. The chain rule handles the composition — differentiate the outside, multiply by the derivative of the inside. It's the workhorse of all real-world differentiation.

PRACTICE: 1) Differentiate f(x) = x³ + 4x² − 7. 2) Use the product rule on f(x) = x²·eˣ. 3) Apply the chain rule to f(x) = sin(2x³).

title: Applications of Derivatives
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Derivatives solve real problems. Optimization: maxima/minima occur at critical points (f'=0 or undefined); the second derivative test classifies them (f''>0 = minimum, f''<0 = maximum). Related rates: differentiate a relationship with respect to time to link changing quantities. Curve sketching: increasing/decreasing (sign of f'), concavity (sign of f''), inflection points. Linear approximation uses the tangent line to estimate. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point where instantaneous rate equals average rate. Newton's method finds roots via derivatives.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Maximize the area of a rectangle with perimeter 20. Area A = x(10−x) = 10x − x². Set A' = 10 − 2x = 0, so x = 5. Since A'' = −2 < 0, it's a maximum. The optimal rectangle is 5×5 (a square), area 25. Calculus turns 'find the best' into solving f'=0 — the single most valuable applied skill in optimization.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the maximum of f(x) = 6x − x². 2) A balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s; find how fast volume grows at r=5 (related rates). 3) Identify where f(x)=x³−3x is increasing.

title: Integration & the Fundamental Theorem
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The integral reverses differentiation — the antiderivative. The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is the signed area under the curve, defined as the limit of Riemann sums. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (the crown jewel): differentiation and integration are inverse operations, and ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative. This connects the two branches and makes areas computable. Basic antiderivatives (reverse the power rule: add 1 to exponent, divide). The '+C' constant of integration for indefinite integrals.

WORKED EXAMPLE: ∫₀² x² dx. Antiderivative of x² is x³/3. Evaluate: (2³/3) − (0³/3) = 8/3 − 0 = 8/3 ≈ 2.67. This is the exact area under y=x² from 0 to 2. The Fundamental Theorem lets us compute this exactly instead of summing infinitely many rectangles — the leap that makes calculus practical.

PRACTICE: 1) Find ∫ (3x² + 2x) dx. 2) Evaluate ∫₁³ x dx. 3) Explain why the '+C' appears in indefinite integrals.

title: Integration Techniques (Calc II)
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Beyond basic antiderivatives, techniques handle complex integrals. u-substitution reverses the chain rule (substitute to simplify). Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du (choose u by LIATE: Log, Inverse-trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Trigonometric integrals and substitution. Partial fractions decompose rational functions. Improper integrals handle infinite bounds or discontinuities via limits. These techniques integrate the functions that arise in physics, probability, and engineering.

WORKED EXAMPLE: ∫ x·eˣ dx by parts. Let u = x (du = dx), dv = eˣdx (v = eˣ). Then ∫x eˣ dx = xeˣ − ∫eˣ dx = xeˣ − eˣ + C = eˣ(x−1) + C. Integration by parts strategically trades a hard integral for an easier one — essential whenever a product of different function types must be integrated.

PRACTICE: 1) Use u-substitution on ∫ 2x(x²+1)³ dx. 2) Integrate ∫ x·cos(x) dx by parts. 3) Explain the LIATE rule for choosing u.

title: Series & Sequences (Calc II)
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: An infinite series sums infinitely many terms. Convergence (sums to a finite value) vs divergence. Tests: geometric series (converges if |r|<1), p-series, ratio test, comparison test, integral test, alternating series test. Power series represent functions as infinite polynomials. Taylor and Maclaurin series approximate any smooth function near a point using its derivatives — the basis for how calculators compute sin, eˣ, etc. Radius of convergence. Series turn transcendental functions into computable polynomials.

WORKED EXAMPLE: The geometric series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... has ratio r = 1/2 < 1, so it converges to a/(1−r) = 1/(1−1/2) = 2. Adding infinitely many terms yields a finite sum — a result that surprised the ancient Greeks (Zeno's paradox) and is now rigorously understood. Taylor series extend this to represent eˣ, sin(x), and more as infinite sums.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the sum of 3 + 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... 2) Determine if Σ 1/n² converges (p-series). 3) Explain what a Taylor series approximates.

title: Grandmaster — Multivariable Calculus (Calc III)
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Multivariable calculus extends to functions of several variables — the mathematics of 3D space and beyond. Partial derivatives (∂f/∂x) measure change in one variable holding others fixed. The gradient ∇f points in the direction of steepest increase (the foundation of gradient descent in machine learning). Multiple integrals (double, triple) compute volume, mass, and probability over regions. Vector calculus: divergence, curl, line and surface integrals, and the great theorems (Green's, Stokes', Divergence) that generalize the Fundamental Theorem to higher dimensions. This is the language of physics and engineering.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For f(x,y) = x²y + y³, the partial derivatives are ∂f/∂x = 2xy (treat y as constant) and ∂f/∂y = x² + 3y². The gradient ∇f = (2xy, x²+3y²) points toward steepest ascent. In machine learning, the negative gradient shows which way to adjust parameters to reduce error — every neural network trains by computing gradients exactly like this, in millions of dimensions.

PRACTICE: 1) Find both partial derivatives of f(x,y) = 3x²y. 2) Explain what the gradient represents. 3) Describe what a double integral computes.

title: King Level — The Depth and Reach of Calculus
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, calculus is revealed as the mathematics of continuous change that underlies nearly all of science. Differential equations (relating functions to their derivatives) model everything dynamic: population growth, heat flow, quantum mechanics, circuits, and economies. The calculus of variations finds functions that optimize integrals (the path of least action in physics). Real analysis provides the rigorous foundation (epsilon-delta proofs) beneath the techniques. Calculus connects to every field: it IS how we describe motion, growth, accumulation, and optimization. The King-level truth: Newton and Leibniz's invention wasn't just a technique — it was a new way of seeing reality as continuously changing and precisely describable, which unlocked the modern scientific and technological world.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Population growth follows dP/dt = kP (rate of change proportional to current size) — a differential equation whose solution is exponential: P = P₀eᵏᵗ. The same equation, with different signs and constants, models radioactive decay, compound interest, and cooling. One calculus relationship describes phenomena across biology, finance, and physics — demonstrating the 'unreasonable effectiveness' of calculus in capturing how the world changes.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain what a differential equation relates. 2) Solve dP/dt = kP conceptually (what kind of function?). 3) Give three different phenomena modeled by exponential change.
